lesson.menu_desc: Perder o turno nao e nao ter o que dizer: sao dois decimos de segundo, e existem frases que os compram
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- Leadership Under Uncertainty
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 19 -- Leadership Under Uncertainty

listenings.text: I chair meetings in three languages, and the thing nobody warns you about is the size of the gap. Between one speaker finishing and the next one starting, English gives you about two tenths of a second. That is not a cultural preference, it is a measurement. Now put a second language on top of it. You hear the end of his sentence, you decide you disagree, you build the first clause in your head, and by the time your mouth opens the gap has closed and somebody else is talking. Nobody interrupted you. You were simply late. So what I tell people is this. Stop composing. Keep four or five openings that need no thought at all, can I come in on that, just to build on what he said, and say one of them before you know what comes next. The sentence will arrive. It always arrives. What will not arrive again is the gap.

We recorded a weekly steering call for six weeks and then did something very boring with it. We counted. Who spoke, for how long, and how many times each person was cut in on. Nobody was accused of anything. There was a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet was the whole intervention. Three of us had eighty percent of the airtime. Two people had been interrupted eleven times between them and had stopped starting sentences at all. They waited to be asked, and mostly they were not. The senior man with the most airtime was the most surprised person in the room, and I believe he was honest about that. He was not dominating anyone on purpose. He simply started faster. Nothing changed because we talked about respect. Things changed because we put a number on a feeling, and once the number existed, the room could not un-see it.
